questions.question: A developer accepts a function suggested by GitHub Copilot and merges it into production. The function later causes incorrect discounts for customers. According to how GitHub Copilot is intended to be used, who is responsible for the code?

options.text: GitHub, because Copilot generated the code
options.why: GitHub does not take responsibility for code that users choose to accept and ship.

options.text: The developer and their organization, because they accepted and shipped the code
options.why: Correct. Accepting a suggestion is the developer's decision, and the code is treated like code they wrote.

options.text: The author of the public repository that the model was trained on
options.why: Training data authors are not responsible for how suggestions are used.

options.text: No one, because AI-generated code is not subject to ownership
options.why: Accepted code becomes part of the codebase, and the team that ships it is accountable for it.

questions.explanation: GitHub does not claim ownership of suggestions, and the developer is responsible for code they accept.

questions.question: A legal team asks whether GitHub claims ownership of code suggestions that GitHub Copilot provides to developers. What is the correct answer?

options.text: GitHub owns all suggestions and grants a license to use them.
options.why: GitHub does not claim ownership of Copilot suggestions.

options.text: GitHub owns suggestions only on Copilot Free.
options.why: Ownership does not vary in this way by plan.

options.text: Microsoft owns suggestions because the models run on Azure.
options.why: Where the models are hosted does not create ownership of suggestions.

options.text: GitHub does not claim ownership of suggestions.
options.why: Correct. GitHub does not claim ownership of Copilot suggestions. The user is responsible for the code they accept.

questions.explanation: GitHub does not claim ownership of suggestions. Ownership of accepted code follows the user's normal arrangements.

questions.question: Which THREE statements describe limitations of code generated by GitHub Copilot? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Suggestions can reference functions or packages that do not exist.
options.why: Correct. Language models can hallucinate APIs and package names.

options.text: Suggestions may not reflect libraries released after the model's training cut-off.
options.why: Correct. The model's knowledge ends at its training cut-off.

options.text: Suggestions are executed and tested by Copilot before they are displayed.
options.why: Copilot does not run or test inline suggestions before showing them.

options.text: Suggestions can contain insecure code patterns.
options.why: Correct. The model learns from public code that includes insecure patterns, and filters catch only some.

options.text: Suggestions are identical every time for the same prompt.
options.why: Model output is non-deterministic and can differ between requests.

questions.explanation: Copilot output can be invented, outdated or insecure, and it is not executed or guaranteed to be repeatable. Review and testing are required.

questions.question: GitHub Copilot suggests adding an npm package that no developer on the team recognizes. What should the developer do first?

options.text: Verify that the package exists, who publishes it, how widely it is used, and its license
options.why: Correct. Suggested packages can be invented or malicious look-alikes, so they must be verified before installation.

options.text: Install the package, because Copilot only suggests packages from verified publishers
options.why: Copilot does not verify publishers, and it can suggest packages that do not exist.

options.text: Ask Copilot to confirm that the package is safe and install it if Copilot agrees
options.why: Copilot can confirm a hallucination with the same confidence. Independent verification is required.

options.text: Add the package to a content exclusion
options.why: Content exclusions control which repository files Copilot uses. They do not evaluate packages.

questions.explanation: Verify every suggested dependency independently. Invented package names are a known risk.

questions.question: A company wants contractual protection related to intellectual property claims arising from GitHub Copilot output. Which action should the company take?

options.text: Enable the Copilot CLI policy for the organization
options.why: The CLI policy controls feature access, not contractual protection.

options.text: Configure content exclusions for all repositories
options.why: Content exclusions limit which files Copilot uses. They do not provide contractual protection.

options.text: Review the terms for its Copilot plan, because Copilot Business and Enterprise terms include IP indemnity
options.why: Correct. Business and Enterprise terms include IP indemnity with conditions, so the company should know what its plan's terms provide.

options.text: Rely on the fact that GitHub claims ownership of all suggestions
options.why: GitHub does not claim ownership of suggestions.

questions.explanation: IP indemnity is part of the Business and Enterprise terms. The conditions are defined in those terms.
